title: QatarEnergy warns Hormuz crisis could delay its LNG expansion projects
excerpt: CEO Saad al-Kaabi told the Qatar Economic Forum that critical equipment cannot reach Qatar, putting the 2027–2028 North Field startup timeline at risk.
body:
• QatarEnergy CEO Saad al-Kaabi said the Strait of Hormuz crisis could delay some of the company's LNG expansion projects, because critical equipment cannot reach Qatar.
  • North Field East trains are due to start in 2027 and North Field South in 2028 — delays would push part of the expected global LNG supply wave further into the future.
  • QatarEnergy is currently producing only a "very minute" volume of liquefied natural gas amid the months-long disruption.
  • Qatar's expansion is one of the largest single additions of liquefaction capacity in the global LNG market, targeting 142 million tons a year by 2030.

QatarEnergy has warned that the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz could delay some of its expansion projects, because critical equipment is struggling to reach Qatar. Chief Executive Saad al-Kaabi made the comments on Sunday at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York, adding that the company was currently producing only a "very minute" volume of liquefied natural gas, Reuters reported.

A few LNG trains under QatarEnergy's North Field East (NFE) expansion are due to start up in 2027, with the North Field South (NFS) expansion set to begin production in 2028, Kaabi said. Any slippage would push part of the expected global LNG supply wave further into the future.

Context & Background

Qatar's gas industry has been at the center of the Middle East conflict that began on Feb. 28, when joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered a crisis that closed the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint through which roughly 20 percent of the world's LNG supply transits. LNG exports from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have been largely halted since; together the two countries hold about 83 million tons a year of liquefaction capacity, including 77 million tons in Qatar, according to the Gas Exporting Countries Forum.

The disruption has gone beyond shipping. Iranian drone strikes hit Qatar's Ras Laffan and Mesaieed industrial cities, damaging two liquefaction trains representing about 13 million tons a year of capacity — units the GECF estimates will need three to five years for full restoration. Work on the North Field expansion itself was suspended when the conflict began, with offshore drilling and platform installation paralyzed by the closure of the strait and the cancellation of war-risk insurance for vessels in the Gulf.

Impact & Analysis

Kaabi's warning marks a shift in how the crisis threatens the gas market. The immediate problem has been moving today's cargoes through a disrupted Gulf; the new risk is that the same crisis interferes with the construction timetable for tomorrow's supply. Qatar's expansion is one of the largest single additions of liquefaction capacity expected anywhere in the world — the company is targeting 142 million tons a year of capacity by the end of 2030, up from 126 million tons once NFE and NFS are complete.

For Asia, where the supply shock is being felt most strongly, delays to new Qatari capacity would tighten an already strained market. India is among the world's largest LNG importers, and Qatar is a cornerstone long-term supplier — any prolonged tightness in global balances translates into costlier spot cargoes and higher import bills for Indian buyers.

Diaspora Angle

The Gulf hosts millions of Indian workers, and Qatar's energy sector alone employs thousands of Indian engineers and technicians. Project delays can ripple into hiring freezes and contract uncertainty for that workforce — worth watching for families in India whose livelihoods depend on Gulf energy jobs.

What's Next

Qatar's energy minister has said LNG capabilities could return to normal within a couple of weeks of the strait reopening, according to The Peninsula Qatar — suggesting the operational halt is reversible, even if the damage to two trains will take years to fix. The more immediate milestone is whether LNG tankers resume regular passage through Hormuz, as OilPrice.com reported this week. Until the strait is reliably open, both current production and the 2027–2028 expansion timeline remain hostage to the crisis.
